analysis.one_liner: Adds sexual orientation and gender identity to federal anti-discrimination protections for jobs, housing, businesses, credit, and juries.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote, despite 50 of 52 Democratic and independent senators signing on as cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The Equality Act would write sexual orientation and gender identity into the major federal civil rights laws, so that LGBTQ people and women are explicitly protected from discrimination in workplaces, housing, stores and services, health care settings, federally funded programs, credit, and jury selection. It also spells out that pregnant workers and transgender people get equal treatment, including access to restrooms and locker rooms consistent with their gender identity, and it says religious freedom law cannot be used as a defense to discriminate under these provisions. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBTQ people and women gain explicit, nationwide statutory protection against discrimination in employment, housing, stores and services (including online retailers and health care providers), federally funded programs, credit, and jury service. Renters, homebuyers, borrowers, workers, and people in the foster system who face refusal of service because of who they are would have a federal legal remedy. The bill also strengthens protections for pregnancy and childbirth in employment.

how_it_helps.text: The bill expands the Civil Rights Act of 1964's public accommodations, employment, education, and federal funding provisions, and the Fair Housing Act, to prohibit discrimination based on sex, sexual orientation, and gender identity [S2] [S3].

It adds stores, online retailers, transportation services, shelters, and establishments providing health care, accounting, or legal services to the definition of public accommodations, closing gaps where LGBTQ people and women could legally be refused service [S2] [S3].
It bans discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity by creditors and in jury selection, areas where no such federal prohibition previously existed in statute [S2] [S3].

It defines sex to include sex stereotypes, pregnancy, childbirth, sexual orientation, gender identity, and sex characteristics, and requires that facilities such as restrooms and locker rooms be accessible consistent with gender identity [S2] [S3].

The bill provides that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act cannot be used as a claim or defense against these anti-discrimination provisions, closing a route by which service refusals could otherwise survive legal challenge [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered businesses and service providers — including religiously affiliated adoption and foster care agencies, shelters, schools, and health care providers — would bear compliance obligations and litigation exposure, and would lose the ability to decline service to LGBTQ people on religious grounds, since the bill bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense [S3]. Employers already subject to the Supreme Court's Bostock ruling would face the same rules in statutory form.
analysis.who_pays_short: Religious service providers and covered businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly overrides the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense under the covered civil rights titles, which religious organizations and faith-based service providers (such as child-placing agencies and schools) argue forces them to act against their beliefs or exit the field [S3].

The public accommodations definition is expanded to cover virtually any provider of goods or services, including online retailers and individual providers, which broadens who can be sued and what conduct is actionable [S3].

The shared-facility rule requires that individuals have access to restrooms, locker rooms, and dressing rooms consistent with their gender identity, a provision critics say displaces sex-separated facilities without case-by-case accommodations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a clear, enforceable national right not to be refused a job, a home, a loan, or everyday services because of who you are — is substantial and applies to a group that current federal statutes do not explicitly cover, even after the Bostock decision. The genuine costs fall on religious service providers and businesses facing new liability, and on anyone who believes sex-specific facilities or faith-based refusals should remain lawful; the bill resolves that conflict in one direction by statute rather than case by case. Whether that trade is worth it is a values question, but the bill is broad and, on the religious-liberty question, deliberately one-sided.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Equality Act in the Senate on June 21, 2023, joined by 49 other Democratic and independent senators as original cosponsors [S3] [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced [S1] [S5].
The action history records no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
The 50 cosponsors included 47 of 48 Senate Democrats and 3 of 4 independents, meaning the entire Democratic-caucus Senate majority supported the bill, but no Senate Republican signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses and faith-based service providers that opposed the new requirements are better off, since no federal anti-discrimination mandate was enacted. LGBTQ people and women remain without explicit nationwide statutory protection outside employment, where the Bostock decision still applies.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Equality Act and led it as lead sponsor

for.name: 47 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the majority leader and committee leadership

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and Senate Republicans' opposition to the measure left it short of the 60 votes needed to advance past a filibuster in a chamber the Democrats controlled 52-48

sides.party_line_note: All 50 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote in the Republican-controlled House or the Senate.

industries.industry: Faith-based child welfare, education, and social service providers
industries.note: The bill would bar them from refusing to serve same-sex couples or LGBTQ people and would strip the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a legal defense, forcing a choice between compliance and exiting government-funded service work. Faith-based foster and adoption agencies were the most directly affected.

industries.industry: Retailers, service businesses, and health care providers
industries.note: They would gain clarity (many already comply with Bostock and state laws) but face expanded public accommodations liability, including for online services, and exposure to discrimination claims. Their interest in avoiding the mandate runs against the public's interest in enforceable anti-discrimination rights.

Employment rules would change little in practice because the Supreme Court's Bostock decision already covers sexual orientation and gender identity under Title VII; the bill would make that protection statutory rather than dependent on a court ruling that could be narrowed.
